PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

**The impact**

The AP page's "0% counted" banner looks like a placeholder rather than real returns, so I can't treat it as results. The newest material I have is the late-October polling and an Oct 31 guide, which suggests the current date may fall before Nov 3, 2026. I still need to pin down the date before drawing any conclusions.

I'm weighing whether the election has actually happened yet, since the AP page still shows 0% counted and the most recent sources I have are from late October. The latest polling I'm looking at is the PPIC September survey, which had Prop 37 ahead 61% to 35%, along with a later PPIC final poll and an AIMSA poll showing it around 59%. I'm also noting endorsements from Newsom and Becerra, though I still need to verify the PPIC final numbers on the source site.

I'm looking at the endorsements and the funding figures now: the Yes side has roughly $35 million behind it, and no committee has reported opposition money as of late October. Polling had it well ahead, so the Yes side looks strongly favored, though support in initiative polls can erode and well-funded opposition often changes outcomes.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side is more likely to win, and the question wants a simple yes or no. Since polling and funding both point toward Yes, the answer would be yes, though a late, well-funded No campaign could still shift things.

I'm going back and forth on whether the user wants the Yes side's chances or a literal yes/no, and I've settled on answering with only "yes" or "no" as requested, even though the phrasing is awkward.

I'm settling on the final answer format: the user asked for only "yes" or "no", so I'll still research further before committing, checking for any results or late opposition that would change the picture.

I'm now planning to check whether anyone has organized opposition to Prop 37, looking at the Taxpayers Association, the Republican Party, and editorial boards, and I'll pull the PPIC October poll directly from its site to confirm the numbers.

I'm noting that the voter guide has no argument submitted against Prop 37, and the summary lists no opponents, which points to weak organized opposition. I want to see who the critics are, mainly the think tanks and housing groups I've guessed at, and whether any "No" committee has formed. I'll check the Secretary of State contribution records and the FPPC filings for any opposition committee.

I'm checking whether any "No" committee formed after October 22, and I'll pull the PPIC October survey from their site to confirm the numbers.

# What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
November 2, 2026 / 6:49 AM PST / CBS Sacramento
California voters will decide the state's next governor, choose candidates for several other statewide offices and weigh in on 14 propositions when they head to the polls on Tuesday.
...
## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

Proposition 40, state’s Billionaires Tax initiative, holds narrow lead among likely voters in the early going
- Californians now inclined to vote No on Proposition 39, the Voter ID initiative - by Mark DiCamillo
Director, Berkeley IGS Poll 
The state ballot initiative that is drawing the most attention in California’s upcoming general election is Proposition 40, the Billionaires Tax initiative.
Nearly three in four likely voters report having already heard of the initiative, and when presented with its official ballot title and summary slightly, slightly more are inclined to vote Yes (48%) than No (41%).
The controversial initiative calls for imposing a one-time 5% tax on the assets of the state’s billionaires, with most of its funds devoted to health care.
The poll finds voting preferences on Proposition 40 to be highly partisan and related to the ideological leanings of the electorate.

November election ballot that are primarily aimed at nullifying the Billionaires Tax should it pass.

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 37 would make homeownership more attainable for middle-class and first-time buyers through low-interest down payment assistance with no cost to taxpayers. They also say it would encourage construction of new homes, increase the housing supply, create jobs, and help families build wealth through homeownership.
No argument against Proposition 37 was submitted for the official Voter Information Guide.

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 37 would make homeownership more attainable for middle-class and first-time buyers through low-interest down payment assistance with no cost to taxpayers. They also say it would encourage construction of new homes, increase the housing supply, create jobs, and help families build wealth through homeownership.
No argument against Proposition 37 was submitted for the official Voter Information Guide.

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

I'm checking the LA Times line about the League of Women Voters opposing the measure, then noting that several major editorial boards, including the Bay Area News Group papers, have come out against it. I'm also weighing that against the view that endorsements matter less than polling and money.

I'm weighing the recent polls on Prop 37: a PPIC sample from mid-October has it at 65 yes to 32 no, and an AIMSA poll from later that month shows 59% yes, with an earlier PPIC reading at 61 to 35. I'm estimating its chances of passing from that lead and the lack of funded opposition, while allowing for late shifts in voter support as opposition builds.

I'm weighing whether the state's sour mood could push voters toward "no" on bond-style measures, though the poll lead still sits at 65%. The turnout drivers on the other propositions, and a likely Democratic-leaning electorate, probably help Prop 37. I'm also considering "ballot fatigue," since many propositions could lead voters to default to "no" on unfamiliar measures.

I'm weighing how voters who default to "no" on unfamiliar bond measures might affect the result, though the ballot title they'd see is fairly clear. Even so, a 65% yes with only a few undecided would require a large late swing to fail, which seems unlikely without a major funded campaign.

I'm comparing past California propositions' final PPIC polls against their actual results, looking at bonds, drug measures, rent control, and minimum wage. Several show the final poll landing close to the outcome, while a few swung noticeably, which tempers how much weight I give a 65% lead.

I'm now going back over how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their actual results, including the 2022 measures on abortion and sports betting and the 2020 ones on property tax and worker classification. Most of the final readings sit close to the outcome, but several swung by ten points or more, which suggests a 65% lead should be treated with some caution.

I'm checking how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their results, and the pattern is that most land close to the outcome. Measures polling above 60% usually pass, though the margin often erodes, as with the 2020 stem cell bond that came in several points below its final poll.

I'm checking how past propositions with final polls near 60% have held up, and the usual pattern is a few points of erosion, which would still leave Prop 37 well above 50%. A failure would take a swing of roughly fifteen points, which happens mainly when one side pours heavy money into the race, as with sports betting or rent control. Given the lack of funded opposition, I'd put the Yes side's chances of winning at around 90%.

I'm wondering whether the election has already happened, so I'm looking for any actual results. The AP page I saw only showed 0% counted, and it looks like a snapshot from before the polls closed, so the current date is probably around election day.

I'm confirming the date from the AP page and the Berkeley IGS note, both dated around November 2, 2026, so the results aren't in yet and this has to be a forecast. I'm also planning one more check for late developments like a poll tightening or a new funded No campaign, since those could change the estimate.

I'm checking a few more things: whether the Yes campaign has any controversies, who funds the "Building a Better California" committee, and whether any new No-side money has appeared in the final week. I'll also look for late spending coverage that could shift the forecast.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Ballot text
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs.

# What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Summary
Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

I'm pulling together the newspaper editorials that came out against Prop 37, from the San Luis Obispo Tribune, the East Bay Times and Mercury News, and the Santa Cruz Sentinel. I'm also checking how the LA Times describes the lack of opposition to it.

I'm checking the LA Times line about the League of Women Voters opposing the measure, then noting that several major editorial boards, including the Bay Area News Group papers, have come out against it. I'm also weighing that against the view that endorsements matter less than polling and money.

I'm weighing the recent polls on Prop 37: a PPIC sample from mid-October has it at 65 yes to 32 no, and an AIMSA poll from later that month shows 59% yes, with an earlier PPIC reading at 61 to 35. I'm estimating its chances of passing from that lead and the lack of funded opposition, while allowing for late shifts in voter support as opposition builds.

I'm weighing whether the state's sour mood could push voters toward "no" on bond-style measures, though the poll lead still sits at 65%. The turnout drivers on the other propositions, and a likely Democratic-leaning electorate, probably help Prop 37. I'm also considering "ballot fatigue," since many propositions could lead voters to default to "no" on unfamiliar measures.

I'm weighing how voters who default to "no" on unfamiliar bond measures might affect the result, though the ballot title they'd see is fairly clear. Even so, a 65% yes with only a few undecided would require a large late swing to fail, which seems unlikely without a major funded campaign.

I'm comparing past California propositions' final PPIC polls against their actual results, looking at bonds, drug measures, rent control, and minimum wage. Several show the final poll landing close to the outcome, while a few swung noticeably, which tempers how much weight I give a 65% lead.

I'm now going back over how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their actual results, including the 2022 measures on abortion and sports betting and the 2020 ones on property tax and worker classification. Most of the final readings sit close to the outcome, but several swung by ten points or more, which suggests a 65% lead should be treated with some caution.

I'm checking how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their results, and the pattern is that most land close to the outcome. Measures polling above 60% usually pass, though the margin often erodes, as with the 2020 stem cell bond that came in several points below its final poll.

I'm checking how past propositions with final polls near 60% have held up, and the usual pattern is a few points of erosion, which would still leave Prop 37 well above 50%. A failure would take a swing of roughly fifteen points, which happens mainly when one side pours heavy money into the race, as with sports betting or rent control. Given the lack of funded opposition, I'd put the Yes side's chances of winning at around 90%.

I'm wondering whether the election has already happened, so I'm looking for any actual results. The AP page I saw only showed 0% counted, and it looks like a snapshot from before the polls closed, so the current date is probably around election day.

I'm confirming the date from the AP page and the Berkeley IGS note, both dated around November 2, 2026, so the results aren't in yet and this has to be a forecast. I'm also planning one more check for late developments like a poll tightening or a new funded No campaign, since those could change the estimate.

I'm checking a few more things: whether the Yes campaign has any controversies, who funds the "Building a Better California" committee, and whether any new No-side money has appeared in the final week. I'll also look for late spending coverage that could shift the forecast.

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

I'm checking whether the Berkeley IGS October poll included Prop 37 among the seven measures it tested, since only one of them reached majority support there. If Prop 37 was below 50% in that poll, it would conflict with PPIC's 65%, so I want to see the actual numbers.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the SurveyUSA poll only covered Props 39 and 40, so it gives no Prop 37 numbers. Turning to the Prop 37 polls I have so far: PPIC's September survey had it at 61–35, and its October survey had it at 65–32. I'm now looking at the AIMSA poll from October 19–24 with 2,000 likely voters, though it isn't a probability sample.

I'm now going through the Mason-Dixon/NBC angle: the newsletter only tied that poll to Prop 40, so it's probably not a Prop 37 source. Weighing the rest of the evidence, I'd put the Yes side's chances around 90%, though I want to check for anything that could reverse that.

I'm weighing the 2026 bond measures, since Prop 37 is a revenue bond rather than a general obligation one and the PPIC poll still shows 65% support. I'm also checking whether early voting or any late "No" money from groups like the Hoover Institution or the mortgage lenders could shift that picture, though neither looks large enough to matter. Next I'm starting to compare it against past California initiatives that held 60%+ in their final polls.

I'm now recalling past California initiatives: the ones with big leads of 60% or more in their final polls usually passed, though a few that polled in the 40s or 50s, like the 2018 rent control and gas tax measures, lost. Prop 37 sits well above that threshold, so the historical pattern supports the Yes side.

I'm now looking at past California initiatives that polled 60% or higher near the end, which mostly passed, though a few like the 2012 Prop 32 and 2014 Prop 37 polled near 50% and lost after heavy spending. Prop 37's lead is well above that range, so that pattern still favors the Yes side.

Weighing a 33-point lead, I'd need a 17-point swing to see Prop 37 fail, and nothing so far points to campaign spending on that scale. That keeps my estimate for a Yes win near 90–93%. One thing still nags at me: the PPIC question may overstate Yes among actual voters if undecided ballots default to No on a complicated measure.

I'm checking whether the measure could have been pulled from the ballot or changed by a legislative deal, but it's on the official voter guide, so that's not a concern. The trend also looks favorable, with PPIC moving from 61% in September to 65% in October. I'll answer "yes," treating this as a forecast since the result isn't known yet.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer, since every reading of the question that I can think of, whether it asks if Prop 37 passes or if the Yes side wins, comes out the same way.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer and checking once more for any post-election results, though everything I've found so far is from before the vote.

I'm checking the 0% counted note against what the index covers, and I'm guessing it stops around Nov 2. I'll run a couple more searches for post-election coverage, like "Prop 37 approved" or "Prop 37 defeated," to make sure nothing's been reported.

...
In his Sept. 21 *Los Angeles Times* column, George Skelton argues that Proposition 37 is a straightforward, taxpayer-free way to help middle-income Californians achieve homeownership by addressing one of the biggest barriers to buying a home: the down payment.
...
Under the proposal, eligible California residents could put down as little as 3% on a newly constructed, owner-occupied home and finance the remaining 17% through a second mortgage.

The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.

A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.

I'm going to check the Oct 29 Berkeley IGS release to see whether Prop 37 was one of the seven measured. I'm also looking at the IGS guide and endorsement table for Prop 37, since the endorsement row seems to have a column that doesn't line up cleanly with the Prop 37 header.

I'm now wondering whether the Bay Area News Group paper broke from the others on Prop 37, since the endorsement row might be misaligned with the headers. The LA Times entry shows a dash, which may mean it hasn't endorsed, or it may not endorse on propositions this cycle. I need to pull the full endorsements table and the IGS Prop 37 guide to sort this out.

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface.
It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes.
Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home.
A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans.
When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk.
That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.

I'm pulling together the newspaper editorials that came out against Prop 37, from the San Luis Obispo Tribune, the East Bay Times and Mercury News, and the Santa Cruz Sentinel. I'm also checking how the LA Times describes the lack of opposition to it.

I'm checking the LA Times line about the League of Women Voters opposing the measure, then noting that several major editorial boards, including the Bay Area News Group papers, have come out against it. I'm also weighing that against the view that endorsements matter less than polling and money.

I'm weighing the recent polls on Prop 37: a PPIC sample from mid-October has it at 65 yes to 32 no, and an AIMSA poll from later that month shows 59% yes, with an earlier PPIC reading at 61 to 35. I'm estimating its chances of passing from that lead and the lack of funded opposition, while allowing for late shifts in voter support as opposition builds.

I'm weighing whether the state's sour mood could push voters toward "no" on bond-style measures, though the poll lead still sits at 65%. The turnout drivers on the other propositions, and a likely Democratic-leaning electorate, probably help Prop 37. I'm also considering "ballot fatigue," since many propositions could lead voters to default to "no" on unfamiliar measures.

I'm weighing how voters who default to "no" on unfamiliar bond measures might affect the result, though the ballot title they'd see is fairly clear. Even so, a 65% yes with only a few undecided would require a large late swing to fail, which seems unlikely without a major funded campaign.

I'm comparing past California propositions' final PPIC polls against their actual results, looking at bonds, drug measures, rent control, and minimum wage. Several show the final poll landing close to the outcome, while a few swung noticeably, which tempers how much weight I give a 65% lead.

I'm now going back over how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their actual results, including the 2022 measures on abortion and sports betting and the 2020 ones on property tax and worker classification. Most of the final readings sit close to the outcome, but several swung by ten points or more, which suggests a 65% lead should be treated with some caution.

I'm checking how past California propositions' final PPIC polls compared with their results, and the pattern is that most land close to the outcome. Measures polling above 60% usually pass, though the margin often erodes, as with the 2020 stem cell bond that came in several points below its final poll.

I'm checking how past propositions with final polls near 60% have held up, and the usual pattern is a few points of erosion, which would still leave Prop 37 well above 50%. A failure would take a swing of roughly fifteen points, which happens mainly when one side pours heavy money into the race, as with sports betting or rent control. Given the lack of funded opposition, I'd put the Yes side's chances of winning at around 90%.

California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.

I'm noting that the SurveyUSA poll only covered Props 39 and 40, so it gives no Prop 37 numbers. Turning to the Prop 37 polls I have so far: PPIC's September survey had it at 61–35, and its October survey had it at 65–32. I'm now looking at the AIMSA poll from October 19–24 with 2,000 likely voters, though it isn't a probability sample.

I'm now going through the Mason-Dixon/NBC angle: the newsletter only tied that poll to Prop 40, so it's probably not a Prop 37 source. Weighing the rest of the evidence, I'd put the Yes side's chances around 90%, though I want to check for anything that could reverse that.

I'm weighing the 2026 bond measures, since Prop 37 is a revenue bond rather than a general obligation one and the PPIC poll still shows 65% support. I'm also checking whether early voting or any late "No" money from groups like the Hoover Institution or the mortgage lenders could shift that picture, though neither looks large enough to matter. Next I'm starting to compare it against past California initiatives that held 60%+ in their final polls.

I'm now recalling past California initiatives: the ones with big leads of 60% or more in their final polls usually passed, though a few that polled in the 40s or 50s, like the 2018 rent control and gas tax measures, lost. Prop 37 sits well above that threshold, so the historical pattern supports the Yes side.

I'm now looking at past California initiatives that polled 60% or higher near the end, which mostly passed, though a few like the 2012 Prop 32 and 2014 Prop 37 polled near 50% and lost after heavy spending. Prop 37's lead is well above that range, so that pattern still favors the Yes side.

Weighing a 33-point lead, I'd need a 17-point swing to see Prop 37 fail, and nothing so far points to campaign spending on that scale. That keeps my estimate for a Yes win near 90–93%. One thing still nags at me: the PPIC question may overstate Yes among actual voters if undecided ballots default to No on a complicated measure.

I'm checking whether the measure could have been pulled from the ballot or changed by a legislative deal, but it's on the official voter guide, so that's not a concern. The trend also looks favorable, with PPIC moving from 61% in September to 65% in October. I'll answer "yes," treating this as a forecast since the result isn't known yet.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer, since every reading of the question that I can think of, whether it asks if Prop 37 passes or if the Yes side wins, comes out the same way.

I'm settling on "yes" as the answer and checking once more for any post-election results, though everything I've found so far is from before the vote.

I'm checking the 0% counted note against what the index covers, and I'm guessing it stops around Nov 2. I'll run a couple more searches for post-election coverage, like "Prop 37 approved" or "Prop 37 defeated," to make sure nothing's been reported.

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

**The impact**
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages.
Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building.
The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
